why: C and D list the six setup conditions so an outsider can scan them (C also spells out cwd and 'variable'), while A opens with a sentence fragment and packs the setup into one line.
All four are the identical bare heading; the order is arbitrary.

A says 'does not start on NixOS' and gives each browser its own version-source bullet with the httpbin check as a separate statement; C and D fold Chromium into Helium's bullet and list the check as if it were a version source, and C's 'None found: the search fails naming' is cryptic.

meaning_problems.C: puts the httpbin check in the list of version sources and merges Chromium into Helium's bullet, blurring what is a source and what is a verification
meaning_problems.D: same list structure as C: the httpbin check reads as a fourth version source

why: A states the upstream sorting bug as cause and effect ('it sorts the names as strings, so 99 beats 156') and keeps the preference sentence separate; D adds a redundant 'to find the newest'; B and C are identical and slightly more compressed.
B labels cause, measurement, consequences and fix and sets the ruling apart so the reader finds each in one glance; D crams the three consequences into one run-on bullet.
B's 'Even so' makes the link between a built-in ad blocker and ads still reaching the DOM explicit; D drops the subject 'Helium' and ends with the clipped 'is for the user'.

D keeps the compact bullet form but spells out 'all three match', 'which rejects everything' and the service worker in full clauses; B is equally clear but wordier; C is the tersest with clipped phrases like 'Rules load'.
C names the tab and says explicitly that newtab is hidden the same way; A's 'hides it' leaves the referent to be inferred.

C turns every parenthetical into a stated cause ('because the rule list is fetched first', 'because the SOCS cookie persisted') and names what R7 means for Bing; A's inverted 'Its search page I only ever saw as /sorry' is the hardest sentence to parse.

B first says what was planted and then what happened with and without --config, so the experiment is reconstructible by an outsider; C's 'Control without --config:' shorthand assumes the reader already knows the setup.

A writes each measurement as a full sentence ('timed out after 3000 / 8000 ms', 'because the daemon doesn't use its own env', 'whether Windows' close_after or a failed batch'); C strips verbs and connectives ('an immediate retry CDP...', '5 of 5 fine') to the point of telegraphese.
The table is identical everywhere; D's prose names what was checked ('the settings for') and contrasts lang with ui_lang/country via 'while', A's semicolon-joined version is the most clipped.
C adds 'queries' to '3 blocks in 10' and 'use' to the config fact, both of which an outsider needs; D drops the comma before 'headless and headed' and compresses 'for all six'.
A and D state the run setup in full sentences and split the Google reasoning into separate sentences; B and C open with a comma-spliced fragment and run the Google evidence into one long sentence.

B keeps the compact per-engine summaries but writes the notes as full sentences ('must classify both as Captcha', 'because Brave never showed either'); C is clear but repetitive in the google bullet; D says the expression 'fires on the first' without naming what.

A alone says unambiguously that none of the scrubbed values is a parser marker and gives the not-obtained consequence as a full sentence; B crams the scrubbing list into one paragraph and, like C and D, ends it with 'No parser marker lives in any of them', whose 'them' can be read as the fixture files.

meaning_problems.B: 'No parser marker lives in any of them' can be read as the fixture files containing no markers rather than the scrubbed values not being markers
meaning_problems.C: same ambiguous 'any of them' after a list of files
meaning_problems.D: same ambiguous 'any of them' after a list of files
